newsitem.title: NORWAY: Guatemala government and rebels sign ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala government and rebels sign ceasefire.

text.p: The Guatemalan government and leftist rebels signed a ceasefire agreement in Oslo on Wednesday, the first of several accords to end Latin America's longest civil war.
Government envoy Gustavo Porras and the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) representative, Rolando Moran, initialled the document that formally ended 36 years of bloody hostilities.

"This is a very special moment. It's a promise for the future," Nobel laureate Rigoberta Menchu, a Mayan Indian, told Reuters after the signing at Oslo's City Hall, where the Nobel Peace Prize is awarded every year.
"It is also a very sad day because of the cost of the conflict. We need to work for the victims and the orphans, for their future," Menchu said.
Menchu won the 1992 Nobel Peace Prize for her struggle for the human rights of the indigenous Guatemalan Indians.
Her mother, father and a brother were killed by the military during the war, in which more than 100,000, mainly civilians, have died and another 40,000 have disappeared.

The ceremony follows more than five years of negotiations, including 11 separate accords on everything from Indian rights, army troop reductions, constitutional and election reforms and the post-war political role of the URNG rebel organisation.
Under the truce, UNRG rebel forces will be disarmed and concentrated in eight locations in interior Guatemala, where they will remain until reintegration into civilian life.
It was the first of three accords to be signed before the final peace agreement on December 29 in Guatemala City.
The government and rebels are scheduled to sign a deal on constitutional and election reforms in the Swedish capital Stockholm on December 7.
They will head to the Spanish capital Madrid on December 12 to complete the treaty on integrating guerrillas into society.
United Nations mediator Jean Arnault said there were still some outstanding differences between the government and rebels, mainly over elections and reintegration.
"But we do believe that with true dialogue and negotiations we will reach a solution," Arnault said.
The parties will return to Mexico before the final signing to finish the negotiations and agree a timetable for implementation of the accords, he said.
Guatemalan Antonio Rosales said after the ceremony that it was a breakthrough the whole of Guatemala had waited for.
"My feelings are of relief. I have been sceptical of this process but all the sides have come here and shown commitment.
"It's a great day and gives us hope that one day we will be able to return to a peaceful and democratic country," said the 40-year-old surgeon, who has lived in Norway for ten years.
Norway has in the past mediated secret negotiations between Israel and the Palestinian Liberation Organisation which led to the signing of the historic Oslo peace accords in 1993.
Oslo hosted an initial round of Guatemalan peace talks in 1990 before the United Nations took over as mediator.
